c: , sometimes also known by the Chinese term

(山寨), describes the look of unauthorized imitations of branded products, including toys, stationery, clothing, packaging, DVD covers, game cartridges, and shop signs. Such products are commonly found at

, street markets, and informal vendors. The Chinafake Wiki separates a "knockoff," which resembles another product or franchise, from a "counterfeit," which is meant to be identical to it, and notes that neither has permission from the original creators. This page mostly concerns knockoffs and bootlegs, because a counterfeit is made to look the same as the original.

This page is broad. The products it covers come from different countries, decades, and price points, and they do not share one uniform look. The features that recur are described below: characters redrawn off-model with slightly wrong or uncanny proportions, packaging art that does not match the product, altered brand names and logos, garbled English, and loud color schemes.

The bootleg look has no single documented origin, and the sources describe separate strands in different places. In the Soviet Union, fake Adidas trainers were being made in the south of Russia in the 1980s, and after 1991 the newly opened markets there filled with Turkish and Chinese clothing, which is the setting for the joke brand name "Abibas." In the United States, The Washington Post reported in June 1990 that young Black people across the country had taken up Bart Simpson through bootleg T-shirts. The Evilstick, a toy wand made in China, was first recorded in a New York store in 2008 and was still sold in discount stores in the United States and New Zealand in 2014.
In April 2013, the architecture blogger Evan Chakroff published a post titled "Bootleg Aesthetics" about the bootleg DVD covers he had been scanning from shops in Shanghai for about six months.

Photographing and collecting bootleg products has also become an online pastime. The collector behind the Bootleg Bart archive began sharing his shirts online after buying his first ones in 2003 for a laugh. The subreddit r/crappyoffbrands, created in 2015, collects photographs of knockoff products from around the world and had over 900,000 members by 2021. The Chinafake Wiki documents knockoff toys, and various YouTube channels entirely dedicated to showcasing bootleg goods such as toys and phones exist. From 2015 to 2018, DISNOVATION.ORG assembled and exhibited
, its collection of shanzhai phones, as a critical look at how technology is produced.

c: Knockoff brands often alter an existing name or mark, not replace it. In a 2024 collection of examples from China, the travel writer China Mike shows Adidas rendered as "Abidas" and "Daiads," an Adidas shoe with four stripes in place of three, Nike rearranged as "Neki" and "Nkie," Birkenstock changed to "Birkin Stick," Converse rendered as "Cnovesre," and shop signs reading "Sunbucks Coffee," "Bucksstar Coffee," and "Abercrombie and Titch." The same collection includes an "X-boy" game system that combines the names of the Game Boy and the Xbox. The name "Abibas" belongs to Russian markets of the 1990s and became a joke in its own right. The Lego imitator Lepin sold a Star Wars-themed set under the name "Star Plan." Fans have carried the wordplay into nicknames of their own, such as "Lafufu" and "Lagogo" for counterfeit Labubu dolls.

c: Bootleg toys often pair a recognizable character with packaging art that was made separately from the toy. Comic Book Resources describes Sailor Moon bootlegs whose box art gets a character's colors right while changing her outfit, and whose toys resemble neither the character nor the picture on the box. The collector site Toy Wizards describes doll lines where the packaging art is the main sign of a fake, with illustration styles and color palettes that change from one product to the next. Cracked's 2011 article on bootleg toys says that makers sold through street vendors and dollar stores change names and designs slightly to get around copyright law. The Chinafake Wiki lists Mickey Mouse, Goku, Naruto, Pikachu, and Mario among the characters copied, and says the toys are made of cheap plastic, carry colorful lights, and sometimes have speaker holes with no speaker behind them.

c: Packaging text on knockoff toys often contains spelling and grammar errors. The Chinafake Wiki gives "It will give you infinite pleasure" as a phrase found on many boxes. Chakroff's post on Shanghai DVD covers also mentions double translations among the features of the covers.
One of the main reasons why grammar may appear poor, often humorously called

, is because manufacturers often do not speak the language of the country where the product will be finally sold (or, alternatively, OCR scanning and machine translation). Rather than prioritizing linguistic accuracy, manufacturers frequently choose specific words based on their emotional appeal or perceived marketability, often translating them literally from dictionaries without considering how the phrases will be received by Western consumers.

This sometimes results in phrases and slogans that consumers find bizarre or unintentionally offensive, such as the infamous "WORLD IS A FUCK" shirt or knockoff versions of branded products like a "Black Power" Oreo's parody.

Chakroff listed oversized fonts, obnoxious colors, action imagery inserted into period films, heavy use of Photoshop filters, and images taken from unrelated movies as trends in the bootleg DVD covers he collected. Paparazzi photographs were clipped and laid over official posters, and the covers became collages of whatever imagery was available. He wrote that the look of particular bootleg production houses could be recognized, and that many covers were branded with a red eagle or an Apple logo.

c: Mobile phones are the products most closely associated with the word

. A 2009 news report described the term as a nickname for low-priced handsets made in Shenzhen, covering any phone not licensed for sale by regulators, including look-alikes of the iPhone and the Nokia N97 that could be hard to tell apart from the originals. The imitation iPhones sold in a Beijing electronics market had 3.5-inch or 2.9-inch screens and showed apps as iPhone-style rounded icons, and they came with Chinese apps such as a popular chat client already installed.

In the 2010s, Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei market sold dozens of phones whose names and shapes echoed the iPhone, lined up in stall after stall in multi-storey malls. They could do things the original could not, such as taking more than one SIM card or using a replaceable battery. The Victoria and Albert Museum collected a dual-SIM fake iPhone 5S in Shenzhen in 2013, which copies the look of the original but runs Android and has a removable back.

wrote in 2018 that dual SIM cards had been available in shanzhai products for over a decade before Apple added them, and that a product could reach shelves in four to six weeks, against 12 to 18 months for a Western company.
Not every shanzhai phone copied a brand. From 2015 to 2018 the art collective DISNOVATION.ORG assembled

, a collection of more than 100 of these phones, and exhibited it in Europe from 2017. The project's press release describes a Buddha Phone that becomes a virtual altar when a key is pressed, a Prisoner Phone billed as the smallest in the world and made almost entirely of plastic, a Taser Phone marketed as a self-defense weapon, and a Sound System Phone made for retirees who dance in public, loaded with old communist songs. It also mentions strawberry-shaped and car-shaped phones and models with built-in electric razors, lighters, power banks, or video projectors. The release, written in 2018, adds that shanzhai might be under threat after the Chinese government decided to clean up the country's reputation for counterfeiting.

c: Mimicry storefronts are shops and restaurants that copy the name, logo, colors, or layout of an established chain, such as fast food restaurants or specific fashion brands. One widely reported case is a group of Apple Store lookalikes found in Kunming in July 2011 by an American blogger who wrote as BirdAbroad. The main shop had the spiral staircase, wooden tables, and staff in blue T-shirts with name badges, and the employees said they believed they worked for Apple. The stairs were poorly made, the walls were badly painted, and the sign read "Apple Store" where Apple's own stores show only the logo. Two other lookalikes stood around the corner, one with a sign that read "Apple Stoer." Apple had no stores in Kunming at the time. Chinese authorities later identified 22 more unauthorized Apple stores in the city and ordered them to stop using the logo, and reports did not establish whether the goods sold were real or counterfeit. After the story spread, readers sent the blogger photographs of similar shops in Costa Rica, Caracas, and Vietnam.

Restaurant chains are copied through altered names and near-identical logos. In Shanghai, Sunbucks Coffee keeps the green and white Starbucks logo but replaces the mermaid with a Chinese dragon. In Iran, the lack of formal diplomatic relations with the United States makes official McDonald's and Pizza Hut branches hard to find. NPR reported in 2013 on copies including Mash Donald's, Pizza Hat, and Raees Coffee, a Starbucks replica. The analyst who counted nine of them said some looked like the real thing, with one Baskin-Robbins copy using the same 31 flavors, cups, and spoons, and that she believed Starbucks had tried without success to sue Raees Coffee. The Pizza Hat logo turns the hut in Pizza Hut's roof into a hat worn by a man. Roundups of knockoff chains list examples in many other countries, including KKFC in Nepal (short for Krispy Krunchy Fried Chicken), a Kazakh restaurant with McDonald's-style arches, McDoner's in the United Kingdom, and Duffin Dagels in Spain, which borrows the pink and orange Dunkin' Donuts colors. Dairy King in Connecticut is a Dairy Queen imitation.

c: In July 2013, a photograph of a shop with a KFC-style logo showing Adolf Hitler in place of Colonel Sanders spread through the news. Andrew Spooner, the author of a Thailand guidebook, had tweeted it as a "Hitler Fried Chicken" shop in Thailand, and he said he had found the photograph online and had not taken it himself. The Daily Mail presented it as a recently opened restaurant in Bangkok and as an example of what it called "

" in Thailand, and Yum! Brands, the owner of KFC, said it was considering legal action. Spooner then said that the Mail's quote from a Bangkok resident was invented and that the shop was not in Bangkok. The Bangkok Post reported that it was in Ubon Ratchathani and was named H-ler, and KFC dropped its threat after learning that the shop had either closed or never existed.

c: Unlicensed T-shirts of Bart Simpson were sold in the early 1990s and became known as "Bootleg Bart" shirts. According to an interview with an archivist of the shirts published by Vice, the designs placed Bart in sports scenes, war scenes, and other unrelated situations, and many showed him as a Black character connected to hip-hop music, rasta culture, and anti-apartheid imagery. The same interview acknowledges that some of these shirts used racist caricatures. The shirts are an American tradition with their own visual conventions and are only loosely connected to the toy and packaging styles above.

Bootleg aesthetics exist at the intersection of illicit manufacturing and working-class consumer choice. Counterfeit products are sold through street vendors, dollar stores, and increasingly online marketplaces, all places where low prices are the main selling point. Affordability is the most-cited reason for purchasing counterfeits, with about 1 in 3 Europeans finding it acceptable when originals are too expensive. Research on low-income consumers in Brazil found that buyers use fakes to access symbolic goods they couldn't otherwise afford, allowing them to participate in consumer culture.

The visual defects described in the Visuals section, such as off-model proportions, garbled text, and mismatched packaging art, are largely byproducts of two pressures rather than fully intentional style choices. The first is cost-cutting: manufacturers use the cheapest available plastics, inks, and printing processes, which produces the poor registration, faded colors, and inconsistent/peeling paint jobs documented in reports on fake toys. The second is the evasion of copyright law: because names/logos/character designs must be altered just enough to avoid triggering an infringement claim, brand names get distorted into puns/misspellings and pop culture characters are replicated from memory or poor-quality photos. This is in stark contrast with officially licensed products, which companies create from official studio art and strict brand guidelines for logos, and part of the reason why the aesthetic strikes consumers the way it does is because of the
effect, even if they can't quite pinpoint why.

cap: Real squishy dumplings (left) versus bootleg counterfeit versions (right). Despite visual similarities, confiscated bootleg dumplings across the UK were found to contain toxic chemicals and benzene, posing serious health risks to children despite their cute and innocent aesthetic.

c: The economic pressures described above that influence bootleg aesthetics visually are also inseparable from what the products are made of. Manufacturers minimizing cost on materials and quality control produce not just "cheapness," but products that can pose real dangers. Bootleg products frequently contain unregulated adhesives, plasticizers, and chemical dyes that would fail safety testing in regulated markets. The strong chemical odor emitted by many bootleg toys and clothing/costumes correlates with off-gassing of volatile organic compounds (VOCs).
Counterfeit toys frequently contain prohibited phthalates and lead. Trading Standards in Warwickshire found fake Maleficent figures containing 18 times the legal limit of phthalates, and fake

dolls seized in Pontefract and West Yorkshire the same year also tested for dangerous phthalate levels, part of a long pattern of contaminated counterfeit toys. This poses serious risk given children's hand-to-mouth behavior and close contact with toys and clothing.

c: Bootleg toys that produce sound generally run on cheap musical integrated circuits, referred to in online communities as "ICs" or "sound chips," rather than on licensed audio recordings. The Chinafake Wiki's catalogue of these chips traces some of them back decades; the siren effect built into a chip labelled UM3561, for instance, had already been used in HESS toy trucks during the 1990s and early 2000s before recurring across newer chinafake products. Because a single chip supplier's product can be installed by many unrelated toy makers, the same clip of music or sound effect resurfaces across otherwise unconnected toys, from cars to flip phones to plush animals.
The most widely circulated example is the chorus of "

group Smile.dk. On the toy phones that popularized it, the chip typically follows a fixed sequence: two rings, a high-pitched voice asking "may I help you?", a dog bark, and then the chorus. A culture writer for Saigoneer reported that a single Chinese manufacturer likely produced most of these chips, which were then bought pre-made and installed by separate toy assemblers, resulting in the "butterfly phone" nickname for the entire toy line regardless of which character or brand appeared on the casing.
Other eurodance and bubblegum dance songs, which had been popularized across East Asia thanks to the rhythm game
, recur across the same category of toy. The Vengaboys' "
Kiss Kiss (When the Sun Don't Shine)
" plays on a separate line of walking and driving toys, while Aqua's "

" have been documented on bootleg Winnie the Pooh figures, and a 2 Unlimited track appears on a Lightning McQueen knockoff. The Chinafake Wiki's fan-documentation pages list further variants using tracks such as "

," credited to different, sometimes fictitious, artist names on the toy packaging. Not every chip carries music; some instead loop plain sound effects, such as sirens, alarms, or a barking dog, with no accompanying song.

Because the manufacturers of individual bootleg toys are rarely identified and the same chips circulate for years across unrelated products, hobbyists have taken to archiving them independently of the toy companies themselves. The Chinafake Wiki cross-references known songs and sound effects against the specific chips that produce them, and a YouTube channel dedicated to the wiki, active since 2014, along with fan-run playlists of ripped chip audio, document these clips outside of the toys that housed them.
